source_policy.authority: Supplied source text is authoritative for source-derived claims.
source_policy.preservation_rule: Preserve meaningful concepts, mechanisms, distinctions, history, examples, references and explicit ecosystem connections from the source; do not silently replace source framing with outside knowledge.

central_system_flows: CLI -> Engine API -> dockerd -> Docker objects
Swarm -> Docker Engines -> services -> Raft majority consensus
container -> volume -> persistent data independent of container lifecycle
Docker on Linux -> host kernel; Docker on macOS -> Linux VM

nodes.label: Docker
nodes.description: Containerization platform using OS-level virtualization to package and run software in containers.

nodes.label: Docker Engine
nodes.description: Core software that runs and manages containers.

nodes.label: dockerd
nodes.description: Persistent daemon managing container objects and serving Docker Engine API requests.

nodes.label: Docker CLI
nodes.description: Command-line client used to interact with Docker daemons.

nodes.label: Docker Engine API
nodes.description: API through which clients send requests to dockerd.

nodes.label: Container

nodes.label: Container Registry

nodes.label: Docker Volume

nodes.label: Image vs Container
nodes.description: Image is a read-only template; container is a runnable managed environment.

nodes.label: Container vs Virtual Machine
nodes.description: Containers share a host kernel; VMs maintain separate guest environments.

nodes.label: Namespaces vs cgroups
nodes.description: Namespaces isolate views; cgroups limit resources.

nodes.label: dockerd vs Docker CLI
nodes.description: dockerd is the persistent daemon; CLI is the user-facing command interface.

nodes.label: CLI vs Engine API
nodes.description: CLI is a client; Engine API is the programmatic request interface served by dockerd.

nodes.label: Registry vs Image
nodes.description: Registry stores/distributes images; image is the packaged artifact.

nodes.label: Compose vs Swarm
nodes.description: Compose coordinates multi-container applications; Swarm clusters Docker daemons and services.

nodes.label: Service vs Container
nodes.description: Service describes/scales containers across daemons; container is the execution object.

nodes.label: Volume vs Container
nodes.description: Volume persists independently of container lifecycle.

nodes.label: Docker Linux vs Docker macOS
nodes.description: Linux can use host kernel directly; macOS uses a Linux VM.

nodes.label: Dockerfile vs Image
nodes.description: Dockerfile is build instructions; image is resulting read-only template.

nodes.label: Push vs Pull
nodes.description: Push uploads an image; pull downloads an image.

nodes.label: Swarm vs Service
nodes.description: Swarm is cluster abstraction; service is scalable workload abstraction inside the swarm.

nodes.label: docker context vs docker stack
nodes.description: Context targets a Docker host; stack manages Swarm services.

nodes.label: Secret vs Volume
nodes.description: Source only establishes secret management and volume persistence; they solve different lifecycle/security concerns.

nodes.label: Docker Engine vs Docker Desktop
nodes.description: Engine is the container engine; Desktop is a desktop product with its own licensing model.

nodes.label: Portability vs Isolation
nodes.description: Packaging enables portability while namespaces/kernel mechanisms provide isolation.

nodes.label: libcontainer vs containerd
nodes.description: libcontainer is a historical direct-kernel component; containerd becomes the default image store component in Engine 29 per source.

equations.name: Container execution model
equations.expression: Container = isolated processes + packaged software/configuration + shared host kernel
equations.meaning: Docker containers encapsulate application processes and dependencies while sharing the host operating-system kernel.

equations.name: Image-to-container relation
equations.meaning: A Docker image stores the packaged application template used to build/run containers.

equations.name: Linux resource control
equations.meaning: cgroups provide resource limiting for CPU and memory.

equations.name: Linux namespace isolation
equations.expression: Container view = isolated(process tree, network, user IDs, mounts)
equations.meaning: Namespaces isolate an application's view of key operating-environment resources.

equations.name: Registry distribution flow
equations.expression: Build -> Image -> push -> Registry -> pull -> Runtime
equations.meaning: Images can be built, uploaded to a registry, then downloaded by clients for use.

equations.name: Compose application flow
equations.expression: Compose YAML -> Services -> Containers -> Multi-container application
equations.meaning: Compose defines service configuration and creates/starts/scales containers.

equations.name: Swarm consensus condition
equations.expression: Commit update only if approvals > N/2
equations.meaning: Source states Swarm uses Raft and a majority of nodes must agree for an update.

equations.name: Container data persistence
equations.meaning: Docker Volume allows data to survive deletion/recreation of a container.

source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

semantic_distinctions.name: Image vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Image is a read-only template; container is a runnable managed environment.

semantic_distinctions.name: Container vs Virtual Machine
semantic_distinctions.description: Containers share a host kernel; VMs maintain separate guest environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Namespaces vs cgroups
semantic_distinctions.description: Namespaces isolate views; cgroups limit resources.

semantic_distinctions.name: dockerd vs Docker CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: dockerd is the persistent daemon; CLI is the user-facing command interface.

semantic_distinctions.name: CLI vs Engine API
semantic_distinctions.description: CLI is a client; Engine API is the programmatic request interface served by dockerd.

semantic_distinctions.name: Registry vs Image
semantic_distinctions.description: Registry stores/distributes images; image is the packaged artifact.

semantic_distinctions.name: Compose vs Swarm
semantic_distinctions.description: Compose coordinates multi-container applications; Swarm clusters Docker daemons and services.

semantic_distinctions.name: Service vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Service describes/scales containers across daemons; container is the execution object.

semantic_distinctions.name: Volume vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Volume persists independently of container lifecycle.

semantic_distinctions.name: Docker Linux vs Docker macOS
semantic_distinctions.description: Linux can use host kernel directly; macOS uses a Linux VM.

semantic_distinctions.name: Dockerfile vs Image
semantic_distinctions.description: Dockerfile is build instructions; image is resulting read-only template.

semantic_distinctions.name: Push vs Pull
semantic_distinctions.description: Push uploads an image; pull downloads an image.

semantic_distinctions.name: Swarm vs Service
semantic_distinctions.description: Swarm is cluster abstraction; service is scalable workload abstraction inside the swarm.

semantic_distinctions.name: docker context vs docker stack
semantic_distinctions.description: Context targets a Docker host; stack manages Swarm services.

semantic_distinctions.name: Secret vs Volume
semantic_distinctions.description: Source only establishes secret management and volume persistence; they solve different lifecycle/security concerns.

semantic_distinctions.name: Docker Engine vs Docker Desktop
semantic_distinctions.description: Engine is the container engine; Desktop is a desktop product with its own licensing model.

semantic_distinctions.name: Portability vs Isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Packaging enables portability while namespaces/kernel mechanisms provide isolation.

semantic_distinctions.name: libcontainer vs containerd
semantic_distinctions.description: libcontainer is a historical direct-kernel component; containerd becomes the default image store component in Engine 29 per source.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker containers are full virtual machines.
misconceptions.correction: Containers share the host OS kernel; they are OS-level virtualization environments rather than separate guest VMs in the Linux model described.

misconceptions.misconception: A Docker image is the running application.
misconceptions.correction: An image is a read-only template; the container is the runtime object.

misconceptions.misconception: Namespaces and cgroups do the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Namespaces isolate views of resources; cgroups limit CPU/memory resources.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker always runs directly on the host kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source states Docker on macOS uses a Linux virtual machine.
Dockerfiles are text build specifications that produce images.

misconceptions.misconception: A registry is a running container.
Compose and Swarm are the same.
misconceptions.correction: Compose manages multi-container applications; Swarm clusters Docker Engines and manages services.

misconceptions.misconception: Deleting a container necessarily deletes persistent data.
misconceptions.correction: Docker Volumes can preserve data independently of container deletion/recreation.

misconceptions.misconception: Swarm updates require one node's approval.
misconceptions.correction: Source states Raft requires majority agreement.
The CLI is a client; dockerd is the persistent daemon.

misconceptions.misconception: EXPOSE alone publishes a port to the network.
misconceptions.correction: Source only states EXPOSE declares a port; it does not state that declaration alone publishes it.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker's Linux runtime has no kernel-level isolation.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly identifies namespaces and cgroups as Linux kernel mechanisms used by Docker.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.
why_it_matters.central_model: Application + dependencies -> Dockerfile/build -> read-only image -> registry distribution -> container runtime -> isolated processes + shared kernel -> Compose/Swarm coordination -> persistent volumes where required.
why_it_matters.central_insight: Docker is best understood as a connected packaging, runtime, distribution and orchestration ecosystem: images define reusable software artifacts, containers instantiate them, the Linux kernel supplies isolation/resource primitives, registries distribute artifacts, Compose coordinates applications, and Swarm clusters Docker Engines.
